items.label: Pilot study
items.title: Does prompt design stop AI models inventing invoice data?
items.subtitle: A pilot test of four prompts on two Claude models
card_paragraphs: I tested whether the way a prompt is written changes how often an AI model gets invoice details wrong or makes them up. Two Claude models read 80 synthetic UK invoices under four prompts, 1,920 tests in total.

Both models read every printed value correctly. The problem was invention: when a field was missing, three of the four prompts filled it in with a plausible guess. One added sentence, "if a field is missing, return null rather than guessing", cut invented values by about 80%.
items.abstract: Businesses increasingly use AI models to read invoices and turn them into structured data. The main risk is not misreading but invention: a confident, plausible value for a field that is not on the page. This pilot study tested whether prompt design changes that risk. Two Claude models (Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5) extracted six fields from synthetic UK invoices under four prompts: plain, structured, few-shot, and structured with a self-check instruction. In the first experiment (960 tests), both models read every printed value correctly, but the first three prompts filled in a missing VAT figure every time, while the self-check prompt never did. A second experiment, planned in advance (960 tests on invoices with missing or inconsistent fields), confirmed the effect: the invented-value rate fell from between 39% and 50% to between 8% and 9%. Field definitions and worked examples gave no improvement over a one-line prompt.
key_findings: Both models read every printed value correctly, under every prompt, including rotated and low-quality scans.
One explicit instruction to return null for missing fields cut invented values from 42 of 90 to 7 of 90 (Opus) and from 35 of 90 to 8 of 90 (Haiku).
Role-setting, field definitions and worked examples made no measurable difference to invention.
items.method: 80 synthetic UK invoices with known correct answers (40 per experiment, including rotated and low-quality scans and invoices with missing or inconsistent fields), each sent as an image to Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 three times under each of four prompts: 1,920 tests. Scoring rules and the second experiment's analysis were fixed before the data was collected; results use cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals and exact McNemar tests. Limits: synthetic invoices, one document type, two models from one provider, and a single run date.
items.card_image_alt: Chart: Bar chart. Invented-value rate on 30 invoices with a missing field. Opus: plain 47%, structured 50%, few-shot 48%, self-check 8%. Haiku: plain 39%, structured 43%, few-shot 40%, self-check 9%.

items.label: Pilot study
items.title: Will an AI hiring screener copy a company's biased decisions?
items.subtitle: A pilot audit of two Claude models
card_paragraphs: Companies customise AI hiring tools by showing them their own past decisions and asking them to "screen consistently". I tested what happens when those past decisions are biased, using fictional CVs and names from a UK government study of hiring discrimination: 3,300 screening decisions across two Claude models.

Out of the box, neither model treated identical CVs differently because of the name. Given a history biased against ethnic-minority names, the larger model called out the discrimination in 93% of decisions and judged on merit instead. The smaller model never mentioned it and pointed to past decisions as its reason. Which AI you use is a fairness decision.
items.abstract: Organisations increasingly customise AI models for hiring by showing them past decisions and asking them to screen consistently. If those decisions were biased, the model might learn the bias. This pilot tested two Claude models (Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5) with fictional CVs for a graduate data analyst role. Used out of the box (1,800 decisions), neither model's shortlisting depended on the candidate's name. A third experiment, planned in advance (1,500 decisions), gave the models a fictional hiring history that was fair, mildly biased or strongly biased against ethnic-minority names, or biased against women through a hidden proxy. The larger model identified the pattern in 93% and 98% of decisions under the strongly biased and proxy histories and judged candidates on merit instead. The smaller model never mentioned the pattern in 750 decisions, and its shortlisting moved towards the bias, though not significantly (p = 0.12).
key_findings: Out of the box, neither model's shortlisting changed when only the candidate's name changed.
Given a strongly biased hiring history, the larger model called out the discrimination in 140 of 150 decisions, and in 147 of 150 when the bias was hidden in a proxy (women's activities).
The smaller model never mentioned names, ethnicity or gender in 750 decisions, cited past decisions in about 70% of them, and drifted towards the bias (not statistically significant in this pilot).
items.method: 15 fictional CVs (strong, average and borderline) for one graduate role, each screened under 10 names taken from the DWP's 2009 field experiment on hiring discrimination, on Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, three times each: 3,300 decisions in total. The biased-history experiment's design, outcomes and tests were written down before any data was collected; analysis uses permutation tests, cluster-bootstrap intervals and Holm adjustment. Limits: the pre-registered primary tests were not significant; fictional CVs and one role; two models from one provider; bias was taught through examples in the prompt, not by retraining the model.
items.card_image_alt: Chart: Grouped bar chart. Fair history: Opus 10%, Haiku 0%. Mild bias: Opus 30%, Haiku 0%. Strong bias: Opus 93%, Haiku 0%. Strong bias plus an instruction to ignore names: Opus 26%, Haiku 0%. Hidden proxy (women's activities): Opus 98%, Haiku 0%.
